This course comprises 144 points, of which 96 points must be from computer science study and 48 points are used to provide additional depth or breadth through elective study.

The course develops through theme studies in: Part A. Foundation studies (42 points), Part B. Professional practice studies (6 points), Part C. Specialist studies (36 points), Part D. Applied studies (12 points), and Part E. Free elective studies (48 points).

Elective units may be at any level, however, no more than ten units (60 points) can be credited to the computer science course at level 1 and a minimum of 36 points must be completed in computer science at level 3.

Note: Students at the Malaysia campus are required to have completed an industry placement in order to graduate. This can either be the Industry-based learning unit (Part E) or a zero credit point unit FIT3199 Industry work experience. This unit will provide a framework for all undergraduate information technology students at the Malaysia Campus to complete the compulsory industry experience as required by the Malaysian Qualifications Agency.

Units are 6 points unless otherwise stated.

Part A. Foundation studies (42 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT1045 Introduction to programming
  • FIT1047 Introduction to computer systems, networks and security
  • FIT1008 Fundamentals of algorithms
  • FIT1058 Foundations of computing
  • FIT2004 Algorithms and data structures
  • FIT2014 Theory of computation
  • FIT2094 Databases*

*If you are in the double degree course with the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours) completing the software engineering specialisation you must replace FIT2094 with a FIT-coded level 2 elective.

Part B. Professional practice studies (6 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT1049 IT professional practice or FIT1055 IT professional practice and ethics


Part C. Specialist studies (36 points)

You must complete one of the following specialisations.

Algorithms and software

You must complete:

a. The following five units (30 points):

  • FIT2099 Object-oriented design and implementation^
  • FIT2102 Programming paradigms
  • FIT2109 Computer science workshop
  • FIT3143 Parallel computing
  • FIT3155 Advanced data structures and algorithms

b. One of the following level 3 elective units (6 points)*: 

  • FIT3080 Artificial intelligence
  • FIT3139 Computational modelling and simulation
  • FIT3146 Maker lab
  • FIT3159 Computer architecture
  • FIT3182 Big data management and processing
  • FIT3196 Computer architecture and networks
  • MTH3170 Network mathematics
  • MTH3175 Network mathematics (Advanced)

^If you are in the double degree course with the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours) completing the software engineering specialisation you must replace FIT2099 with a Level 2 or above FIT-coded elective.

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Artificial intelligence

You must complete:

a. The following five units (30 points):

  • FIT1061 Introduction to artificial intelligence
  • FIT2111 Symbolic artificial intelligence and machine learning
  • FIT2112 Deep learning
  • FIT3191 Generative artificial intelligence
  • FIT3203 Intelligent agents

b. One of the following elective units (6 points)*:

  • FIT3192 Emerging and advanced topics in artificial intelligence
  • FIT3183 Malicious AI and dark side security

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Cybersecurity

You must complete:

a. The following five units (30 points):

  • FIT1057 Introduction to cybersecurity
  • FIT1093 Cybersecurity tools and techniques
  • FIT2173 Software security
  • FIT3185 Privacy enhancing technologies
  • FIT3186 Vulnerability analysis, response and mitigation

b. One of the following level 3 elective units (6 points)*:

  • FIT3031 Network security
  • FIT3168 IT forensics

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Data science

You must complete:

a. The following four units (24 points):

  • FIT1043 Introduction to data science
  • FIT2086 Modelling for data analysis
  • FIT2179 Data visualisation
  • FIT3152 Data analytics

b. Two of the following level 3 elective units (12 points)*:

  • FIT3003 Business intelligence and data warehousing
  • FIT3154 Advanced data analysis
  • FIT3181 Deep learning
  • FIT3182 Big data management and processing
  • FIT3183 Malicious AI and dark side security

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace one level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Part D. Applied studies (12 points)

You must complete one of the following options.

Clayton students - you must complete a full-year project (12 points) relevant to your specialisation, or the industry-based learning placement unit (18 points).

Malaysia students - you must complete a full-year project (12 points) relevant to your specialisation and the industry-based learning placement unit (18 points) or the industry work experience unit (0 points):

Algorithms and software

  • FIT3161 Computer science project 1
  • FIT3162 Computer science project 2

Artificial intelligence

  • FIT3193 Artificial intelligence project 1
  • FIT3194 Artificial intelligence project 2

Cybersecurity

  • FIT3188 Cybersecurity project 1
  • FIT3189 Cybersecurity project 2

Data science

  • FIT3163 Data science project 1
  • FIT3164 Data science project 2

OR

Industry-based learning placement (18 points):

FIT3045 is available only if you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program. 

For Clayton students - If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will complete FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 credit points) and FIT2108 Industry-based learning (0 credit points); or FIT3045, FIT2108 and one of FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 credit points) or FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 credit points) (depending on the duration of your placement). This will replace the Applied studies project units and the Level 3 elective unit in your specialisation.

For Malaysia students - Students at the Malaysia campus are required to have completed an industry placement in order to graduate as required by the Malaysian Qualifications Agency. This can either be FIT3045 Industry based learning (if you are selected to participate) or FIT3199 Industry work experience. Note: You must complete FIT3199 over the Summer vacation period between second and third year.

If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will complete FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 credit points) which will replace the Level 3 elective unit (6 credit points) in your specialisation and two free electives (12 credit points). 

All students in the IBL program must complete a unit over summer semester or overload in one semester by one unit in order to complete the degree within three years (this is because you only complete 18 credit points of credit during the IBL placement semester). You must have completed at least three semesters of your course before starting your IBL placement.

  • FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 points)
  • FIT2108 Industry based learning seminar (0 points)
  • FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 points)
  • FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 points)
  • FIT3199 Industry work experience** (0 points)


Part E. Free elective studies (48 points)

Your elective units may be chosen from the faculty or across the University as long as you have completed the prerequisites and there are no restrictions on enrolment in the units, including choosing to complete a major or minor from other courses. The units may be at any level, however, no more than 10 units (60 points) at level 1 may be credited to the Bachelor of Computer Science and a minimum 36 points must be at level 3.

If you are in a double degree course, some units required for the partner degree are credited as electives towards the computer science degree.

The course develops through the themes of computer science foundation studies, professional practice studies, specialist studies and applied studies 

Part A. Foundation studies

This study will develop your understanding of the role and theoretical basis of computer science and computational methods.

Part B. Professional practice studies

This study develops professional skills by providing an understanding and appreciation of the ethical and professional guidelines applicable to computer science, developing the ability to work as an effective team member, developing the ability to communicate proficiently and appropriately for professional practice, and developing formal project management skills.

Part C. Specialist studies

This study will develop your in-depth knowledge of the specific computer science methods of your specialised field within computer science. You will also develop your ability to apply appropriate methodologies in computer science and develop efficient computational solutions, strong problem-solving skills and the ability to apply analytical thinking.

Part D. Applied studies

The above knowledge and skills are integrated and consolidated in applied practice as demonstrated in a computer or data science project, and in some cases in an industry-based learning placement.

Part E. Free elective studies

These elective units will enable you to broaden and deepen your knowledge of computer science, or to select units from across the University in which you are eligible to enrol.

If you are in a double degree courses, some units required for the partner degree are credited as electives towards the computer science degree.

Course progression map

The course progression map (Clayton) (Malaysia) provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

The Bachelor of Computer Science is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with in-depth computing knowledge. It focuses on software, hardware and the underlying theory of computing and its applications to scientific and technical problem-solving and to information processing in commerce and industry. The Bachelor of Computer Science is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

The Bachelor of Computer Science in Artificial Intelligence is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with in-depth knowledge in AI theory and applications. This specialisation immerses students in key AI topics such as knowledge representation and reasoning, machine learning, neural networks, computer vision, natural language processing, generative methods, and advanced topics including multi-agent systems and quantum machine learning. Students engage in hands-on full-year project to apply AI theories to practical scenarios, ensuring they are well-prepared for real-world challenges. Ethical considerations and the societal impacts of AI are emphasized, equipping graduates to innovate responsibly in the AI field. The Bachelor of Computer Science in Artificial Intelligence is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

The Bachelor of Computer Science in Cybersecurity is an undergraduate degree. This course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with in-depth computing and cybersecurity knowledge. This degree equips graduates with profound knowledge in cybersecurity, encompassing vital areas such as software security, information security, privacy-enhancing technologies, and vulnerability assessment and mitigations. It focuses on both the theoretical underpinnings and practical applications of securing digital infrastructure, protecting data integrity, and understanding cybersecurity laws and ethics. The Bachelor of Computer Science in Cybersecurity is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

The Bachelor of Computer Science in Data Science is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with in-depth computing and data science knowledge. It focuses on software, hardware and the underlying theory of computing and its applications to scientific and technical problem-solving and to information processing in commerce and industry. The Bachelor of Computer Science in Data Science is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

The Bachelor of Computer Science in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with in-depth computing, data science and artificial intelligence knowledge. It focuses on software, hardware and the underlying theory of computing and its applications to scientific and technical problem-solving and to information processing in commerce and industry. The Bachelor of Computer Science in Data Science and AI is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

These course outcomes are aligned with the Australian Qualifications Framework level 8 and Monash Graduate Attributes.

Upon successful completion of the Bachelor of Computer Science it is expected that students will be able to:

1. demonstrate knowledge of the role of computer science and computational methods, and recognise the importance of theoretical underpinning for practical work

2. demonstrate understanding of ethical and legal issues in the chosen specialisation and its historical, contemporary and likely future scientific, industrial and social context

3. analyse problems, design algorithms to solve them, and program efficient software solutions

4. apply problem solving strategies to develop efficient solutions in their area of specialisation; in particular:

  • computer science students will be able to design and implement substantial pieces of software using a range of programming paradigms, advanced data structures and algorithms
  • data science students will be able to design, implement and apply methods for capturing, managing and analysing data


5. communicate and coordinate proficiently by: listening, speaking, reading and writing English and utilising diagrams, graphics and interactive visualisations for professional practice; working as an effective member or leader of teams; and using basic tools and practices of formal project management

6. manage time and processes effectively by prioritising competing demands to achieve personal and team goals, with regular review of personal performance as a primary means of managing continuing professional development; behave in an ethical and professional manner; and be able to adapt readily to changing technologies.

All applicants must satisfy the equivalence of the VCE subject prerequisites.

VET Diploma graduates: To be considered, applicants who are applying with a diploma, in any field of study, will require a minimum average result of at least 60%. Preference will be given to students whose prior studies are related to the course in which they are seeking admission. Programs that involve competency-based assessment without grades or marks will not meet the admission requirements. IT related diplomas may receive up to a maximum of 48 points of first year level credit.

VET Certificate IV graduates: Preference will be given to students whose prior studies are related to the course in which they are seeking admission. To be considered, applicants will normally require at least 70% average. Programs that involve competency-based assessment without grades or marks will not meet the admission requirements.

University course transfers:

  • Applicants who already meet the minimum entry requirements of the course with their previous Year 12 (or equivalent) qualification require at least two completed university units with at least a 60% average to be considered for admission.
  • Applicants who do not meet the minimum entry requirements of the course with their previous Year 12 (or equivalent) qualification must complete at least one academic year with at least a 60% average.

STAT: The STAT can be used to complement an applicant's overall academic background. It cannot be used as the sole pathway of admission into the course.

The Bachelor of Computer Science course can be taken in combination with the following courses:

  • Bachelor of Commerce
  • Bachelor of Engineering (Honours)
  • Bachelor of Laws (Honours)
  • Bachelor of Science
  • Bachelor of Business and Commerce 

This will lead to the award of two degrees, your chosen specialist computer science degree (Bachelor of Computer Science, Bachelor of Computer Science in Artificial Intelligence, Bachelor of Computer Science in Cybersecurity, Bachelor of Computer Science in Data Science) and the degree awarded by the partner course.

Note:

  • the double degree course with the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours) is only available with the algorithms and software specialisation and the electrical and computer systems engineering specialisation, robotics and mechatronics specialisation and software engineering specialisations.
  • the double degree course with the Bachelor of Business and Commerce is only available with the Algorithms and software specialisation.

The requirements for the award of each of the degrees are generally the same whether the award is earned through a single or double degree course, in the case of the double degree with engineering, this is achieved by cross crediting of some study. You should refer to the relevant double degree handbook entry and the course map for the specific requirements.

The course is designed for students who wish to study computing in depth. Computer science is the theory and practice of applying computers and software to problem-solving. Its practical applications span all disciplines including science, engineering, business and commerce, creative and performing arts and the humanities. You will learn how to think like a computer scientist about processes and their descriptions. This will enable you to design algorithms (instructions for computers) and data structures (ways to store information). You will also acquire practical programming skills to implement these in efficient software that solves real-world problems. The course provides strong foundations in the theory of computation and its connection to mathematics.

This flexible course offers you a choice of four specialisations in; algorithms and software studies including graphics, intelligent systems and networks; artificial intelligence with machine learning, deep neural networks, natural language processing, generative methods and computer vision, complemented by ethical considerations; cybersecurity including tools and techniques, fundamental privacy concepts and secure software and network systems; or specialisations in data science or data science and artificial intelligence to handle the massive datasets of the information age. Your studies will conclude with a significant project in the area of your specialisation.

If you are an eligible student, you may apply for the industry-based learning (IBL) placement program as part of the curriculum. Through the IBL placement program you will apply the computer science skills and knowledge you have gained to real-world problems in a professional organisation.

The course is designed for students who wish to study computing in depth. Computer science is the theory and practice of applying computers and software to problem-solving. Its practical applications span all disciplines including science, engineering, business and commerce, creative and performing arts and the humanities. You will learn how to think like a computer scientist about processes and their descriptions. This will enable you to design algorithms (instructions for computers) and data structures (ways to store information). You will also acquire practical programming skills to implement these in efficient software that solves real-world problems. The course provides strong foundations in the theory of computation and its connection to mathematics.

This flexible course offers you a choice of four specialisations in; algorithms and software studies including graphics, intelligent systems and networks; artificial intelligence with machine learning, deep neural networks, natural language processing, generative methods and computer vision, complemented by ethical considerations; cybersecurity including tools and techniques, fundamental privacy concepts and secure software and network systems; or specialisations in data science or data science and artificial intelligence to handle the massive datasets of the information age. Your studies will conclude with a significant project in the area of your specialisation.

If you are an eligible student, you may apply for the industry-based learning (IBL) placement program as part of the curriculum. Through the IBL placement program you will apply the computer science skills and knowledge you have gained to real-world problems in a professional organisation.

This course comprises 48 points: Part A. Coursework (24 points) and Part B. Research (24 points)

Units are 6 points unless otherwise indicated.

Part A. Coursework (24 points)

You must complete:

a. the following unit:

  • FIT4005 Research methods in information technology

b. three elective units (18 points)* from level 4 or level 5 units approved by the faculty honours coordinator (this elective list may change from time to time and vary by campus)

You may be permitted to do one elective unit (6 points) in selected topics (you will enrol in FIT4008 Reading unit), with permission from the thesis supervisor and honours coordinator.

* A maximum of one unit (6 points) may be selected from units offered by other faculties with the approval of the honours coordinator. Suitable units can be identified using the [[http://www. monash. edu. au/pubs/handbooks/units/search][browse units]] tool in the Handbook.

Part B. Research (24 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT4441 Honours thesis part 1
  • FIT4442 Honours thesis part 2
  • FIT4443 Honours thesis part 3
  • FIT4444 Honours thesis final

The Bachelor of Computer Science (Honours) is an undergraduate award. The course is taught in English. Graduates have acquired appropriate research skills and understand the fundamentals of conceptual, methodological and implementation issues of computer science-related research. They have demonstrated a capacity to design, frame and conduct a research project and to communicate their findings to a high standard. This course takes one year of full-time study, or part-time equivalent, and comprises a fourth year of study following the completion of the normal requirements of the Bachelor of Computer Science degree or equivalent. The Bachelor of Computer Science (Honours) is a Level 8 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations

These course outcomes are aligned with the Australian Qualifications Framework level 8 and Monash Graduate Attributes.

Upon successful completion of this course it is expected that students will be able to:

1. demonstrate a knowledge of a range of specialised topics in computer science including historical, cultural, social, legal and ethical issues inherent in research applicable to the discipline of computer science

2. plan, conduct and manage an independent research project

3. evaluate and select research methodologies appropriate to computer science, and demonstrate their uses and limitations

4. critically analyse research literature

5. analyse, synthesise and evaluate factors in a research project

6. document and communicate research results, and the methods used, orally and in a written report

7. undertake independent learning and apply analytical thinking.

This course comprises 192 points, of which 144 points must be from computer science study and 48 points are used to provide additional depth or breadth through elective study.

The course develops through theme studies in: Part A. Foundation studies (48 points); Part B. Professional practice studies (12 points), Part C. Specialist studies (42 or 48 points) and Part D. Applied studies (12 or 18 points); and Part E. Research studies (24 points); and Part F. Free elective studies (48 points).

Elective units may be at any level, however, no more than ten units (60 points) can be credited to the computer science advanced course at level 1 and a minimum of 36 points must be completed in computer science or data science at each of level 3 and 4 (or higher).

Units are 6 credit points unless otherwise stated.

Part A. Foundation studies (48 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT1053 Introduction to programming (Advanced)
  • FIT1054 Fundamentals of algorithms (advanced)
  • FIT1047 Introduction to computer systems, networks and security
  • FIT1049 IT professional practice
  • FIT1058 Foundations of computing
  • FIT2004 Algorithms and data structures
  • FIT2014 Theory of computation
  • FIT2094 Databases

Parts B. Professional practice studies (12 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT2083 Innovation and research in computer science
  • FIT2082 Computer science research project

Part C. Specialist studies (42 or 48 points)

You must complete one of the following specialisations (30 or 36 points**); and two level 4 or level 5 elective units (12 points) as approved by the course director.

Algorithms and software

You must complete:

a. The following five units (30 points):

  • FIT2099 Object-oriented design and implementation
  • FIT2102 Programming paradigms
  • FIT2109 Computer science workshop
  • FIT3143 Parallel computing
  • FIT3155 Advanced data structures and algorithms

b. one of the following level 3 elective units (6 points)*: 

  • FIT3080 Artificial intelligence
  • FIT3139 Computational modelling and simulation
  • FIT3146 Maker lab
  • FIT3159 Computer architecture
  • FIT3182 Big data management and processing
  • FIT3196 Computer architecture and networks
  • MTH3170 Network mathematics
  • MTH3175 Network mathematics (Advanced)

* If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Artificial intelligence

You must complete:

a. The following five units (30 points):

  • FIT1061 Introduction to artificial intelligence
  • FIT2111 Symbolic artificial intelligence and machine learning
  • FIT2112 Deep learning
  • FIT3191 Generative artificial intelligence
  • FIT3203 Intelligent agents

b. One of the following elective units (6 points)*:

  • FIT3192 Emerging and advanced topics in artificial intelligence
  • FIT3183 Malicious AI and dark side security

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Cybersecurity

You must complete:

a. the following five units (30 points):

  • FIT1057 Introduction to cybersecurity
  • FIT1093 Cybersecurity tools and techniques
  • FIT2173 Software security
  • FIT3185 Privacy enhancing technologies
  • FIT3186 Vulnerability analysis, response and mitigation

b. one of the following level 3 elective units (6 points):

  • FIT3168 IT forensics
  • FIT3031 Network security

If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace this Level 3 elective unit with 6 credit points of the 18 credit point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Data science

You must complete:

a. The following four units (24 points):

  • FIT1043 Introduction to data science
  • FIT2086 Modelling for data analysis
  • FIT2179 Data visualisation
  • FIT3152 Data analytics

b. Two of the following level 3 elective units (12 points)*:

  • FIT3003 Business intelligence and data warehousing
  • FIT3154 Advanced data analysis
  • FIT3181 Deep learning
  • FIT3182 Big data management and processing
  • FIT3183 Malicious AI and dark side security

*If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will replace one level 3 elective unit with 6 points of the 18 point IBL unit (FIT3045).

Part D. Applied studies (12 or 18 points)

You must complete a full-year project (12 points) relevant to your specialisation, or the industry-based learning placement (18 points).

Algorithms and software

  • FIT3161 Computer science project 1
  • FIT3162 Computer science project 2

Artificial intelligence

  • FIT3193 Artificial intelligence project 1
  • FIT3194 Artificial intelligence project 2

Cybersecurity

  • FIT3188 Cybersecurity project 1
  • FIT3189 Cybersecurity project 2

Data science

  • FIT3163 Data science project 1
  • FIT3164 Data science project 2

OR

Industry-based learning placement (18 points)

FIT3045 is available only if you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program.

If you are selected to participate in the IBL placement program you will complete FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 credit points) and FIT2108 Industry-based learning (0 credit points); or FIT3045, FIT2108 and one of FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 credit points) or FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 credit points) (depending on the duration of your placement). This will replace the Applied studies project units and the Level 3 elective unit in your specialisation.

All students in the IBL program must complete a unit over summer semester or overload in one semester by one unit in order to complete the degree within four years (this is because you only complete 18 credit points of credit during the IBL placement semester). You must have completed at least three semesters of your course before starting your IBL placement.

  • FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 points)
  • FIT2108 Industry based learning seminar (0 points)
  • FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 points)
  • FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 points)

Part E. Research studies (24 points)#

You must complete the following units.

Note: To progress to Honours you are required to maintain at least a distinction average (70%) throughout your course. If you do not meet this standard you will be required to transfer to C2001 Bachelor of Computer Science or C2000 Bachelor of Information Technology.

  • FIT4441 Honours thesis part 1
  • FIT4442 Honours thesis part 2
  • FIT4443 Honours thesis part 3
  • FIT4444 Honours thesis final

Part F. Free elective studies (48 points)

Your elective units may be chosen from the Faculty of Information Technology, or from across the University; or you may choose to complete a major or minor from the Faculty of Information Technology or other courses, as long as you have the prerequisites and there are no restrictions on enrolment in the units.

Note: If you are doing the Cybersecurity specialisation you cannot do the Cybersecurity minor.

To enhance your IT studies the Faculty recommends the following minors and elective units which can be taken as part of your free electives. Other IT minors are also available, check the Faculty Handbook pages.

Note: If you are doing the Cybersecurity specialisation you cannot do the Cybersecurity minor.

Discipline elective studies

  • Business information systems (minor)
  • Cybersecurity (minor)
  • Games design (minor)
  • Games development (minor)
  • Software development (minor)
  • FIT3190Work professional placement
  • FIT3195Deep tech entrepreneurship

The course develops through the themes of computer science foundation studies, specialist discipline knowledge, research skills, and professional skills, which come together in applied practice.

Part A. Foundation studies

This study will develop your understanding of the role and theoretical basis of computer science and computational methods.

Part B. Professional practice studies

This study develops professional skills by providing an understanding and appreciation of the ethical and professional guidelines applicable to computer science practice and research; developing the ability to work as an effective team member and to communicate proficiently and appropriately in professional and research contexts.

Part C. Specialist studies

This study will develop deep knowledge and advanced skills in advanced computer science or data science.

Part D. Applied studies

The above knowledge and skills are integrated and consolidated in applied practice as demonstrated in a computer science, cybersecurity or data science and AI project, and in some cases in an industry-based learning placement.

Part E. Research studies

This study develops the ability to critically evaluate IT research and to apply appropriate methodologies to conduct independent research in computer science, cybersecurity or data science and AI. It develops strong problem-solving skills and the ability to apply analytical thinking.

Part F. Free elective studies

These elective units will enable you to broaden and deepen your knowledge of computer science or data science, or to select units from across the University in which you are eligible to enrol.

The course progression map provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

The Bachelor of Computer Science Advanced (Honours) is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes four years of full-time study or eight years of part-time study. The degree provides graduates with research and advanced IT development skills. It provides a strong foundation in information technology leading to algorithms and software; cybersecurity or data science and artificial intelligence studies and is a research-focused degree that combines on-campus study with an industry-based learning work placement. Upon successful completion of the Bachelor of Computer Science Advanced (Honours) it is expected that students will be able to:

2. demonstrate understanding of ethical issues in professional and research practice and its historical, contemporary and likely future scientific, industrial and social context

3. critically analyse problems, design algorithms to solve them, program efficient software solutions and demonstrate the ability to transform and apply computational solutions to new context

4. apply problem-solving strategies to design, implement and critically evaluate substantial pieces of software using a range of programming paradigms, advanced data structures and algorithms

5. communicate and coordinate proficiently by: listening, speaking, reading and writing English and utilising diagrams, graphics and interactive visualisations in a professional and research context; working as an effective member or leader of teams; and using basic tools and practices of formal project management

6. plan and execute projects with some independence and take responsibility for your own learning and practice; manage your own time and processes effectively by prioritising competing demands to achieve personal and team goals, with regular review of personal performance as a primary means of managing continuing professional development; behave in an ethical and professional manner, and be able to adapt readily to changing technologies

7. critically evaluate IT research; be able to apply appropriate research methodologies to conduct significant independent research.

Bachelor of Computer Science Advanced (Honours)

","honours_entry_requirements":"","overview":"

The course is an advanced version of the Bachelor of Computer Science, designed for high-achieving students who wish to study computing in depth with a strong research component through the four years of study. Computer science is the theory and practice of applying computers and software to problem solving. Its practical applications span all disciplines including science, engineering, business and commerce, creative and performing arts and the humanities. You will learn how to think like a computer scientist about processes and their descriptions. This will enable you to design algorithms (instructions for computers) and data structures (ways to store information). You will also acquire practical programming skills to implement these in efficient software that solves real-world problems, as well as strong foundations in the theory of computation and its connection to mathematics.

This advanced course will prepare you for either postgraduate study or employment requiring research and advanced computer science skills. You will do a research project unit in your second year, supported by a research skills unit. If you are an eligible student, you may apply for the industry-based learning (IBL) placement program as part of the curriculum or you will complete a two semester capstone project in your chosen specialisation. 

Your studies will conclude with a full-year honours-level research project in a specialist area of advanced computer science or data science. You will graduate with strong research, analysis, problem solving, communication and teamwork skills, deep knowledge of the field of computer science, and hands-on experience in IT research.

You must complete units as specified in Parts A, B and C (144 points): a minimum of 96 points of information technology study over Part A and Part B, and 48 points of free electives in part C.

In choosing units you must ensure that you complete no more than 10 level one units (60 points), and at least six units (36 points) at level 3 of which at least four (24 points) are Bachelor of Information Technology listed (FIT-coded) units.

Units are 6 points unless otherwise specified.

Part A. Specified studies (48 points)

  • You must complete 36 credit point of core units.
  • You must complete 12 credit points of Applied studies as applicable to your chosen major; or the industry-based learning placement (18 credit points)

Core studies (36 points):

  • FIT1045 Introduction to programming
  • FIT1047 Introduction to computer systems, networks and security
  • FIT1049 IT professional practice
  • FIT2001 Systems development
  • FIT2002 IT project management
  • FIT2094 Databases*

Note: If you are in the double degree course with the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours) completing the software engineering specialisation, you must replace FIT2094 with a FIT-coded level 2 elective.

Applied studies for Applied cybersecurity, business information systems, and software development majors:

  • FIT3047 Industry experience studio project 1 and FIT3048 Industry experience studio project 2

 OR

Applied studies for Games and immersive media major:

  • FIT3039 Studio project 1 and FIT3040 Studio project 2

OR

Professional placement

FIT3045 is only available if you are selected to participate in the Industry Based Learning placement program. [https://www.monash.edu/it/industry-based-learning]

If you are selected for the IBL program you will complete FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 credit points) and FIT2108 Industry-based learning (0 points); or FIT3045 (18 credit points), FIT2108 (0 points) and either FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 points) or FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 points) (depending on the duration of your placement). The IBL placement will replace your Applied studies project units and the nominated Level 3 unit in your major.

In the IBL program you must complete a unit over summer semester or overload in one semester by one unit in order to complete the degree within three years (this is because you only complete 18 credit points of credit during the IBL placement semester). You must have completed at least three semesters of your course before starting your IBL placement.

  • FIT3045 Industry-based learning (18 points)
  • FIT2108 Industry based learning seminar (0 points)
  • FIT3201 Industry-based learning onboarding (8 weeks) (0 points)
  • FIT3202 Industry-based learning onboarding (4 weeks) (0 points)


B. Major studies (48 points)

You must complete at least one information technology listed major. A major requires eight units with no more than two units at level one (12 points) and at least three units (18 points) at level three. 

Minors and majors  Refer also to the table of minors, majors and extended majors by campus which also details if an area of study is available as a minor, major or extended major.


C. Free elective studies (48 points)

Your elective units may be chosen from any of the units offered at Monash to suit your interests or career aspirations. For example, you may choose to take other units available in the Bachelor of Information Technology course to extend your major or to complete a second major or minor(s) from the course, or you may take faculty of IT units from C2001 Bachelor of Computer Science or the software engineering specialisation in the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours). Elective units may also be used to sample from across the University or to complete a major or minor(s) from another course as long as you have completed the prerequisites and there are no restrictions on enrolment in the units.

If you are in a double degree courses, some units required for the partner degree are credited as electives towards this degree.

This is a comprehensive course, structured in three equal parts:

Part A. Specified studies

This will provide you with foundation skills and knowledge for your IT education and ensure a breadth of understanding of IT and its applications in organisations and society.

Part B. Major studies

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your expertise in one area of information technology. You will develop the practical and theoretical skills and knowledge in your chosen major needed to successfully plan, develop, implement and evaluate information products and systems.

Part C. Free elective studies

Electives will enable you to further develop your knowledge of your major area of study, or IT more broadly, through a second major or a minor. Alternatively you can select units from across the University in which you are eligible to enrol.

If you are in a double degree course, some units required for the partner degree are credited as electives towards the information technology degree.

Course progression map

The course progression map provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

The Bachelor of Information Technology is an undergraduate degree. The course is taught in English and normally takes three years of full-time study or six years of part-time study. It is designed for students who wish to study the application of computer-based technologies and systems to meet individual and organisational information needs. It is a highly practical course which prepares graduates for careers working with information and IT in business, government and industry. The Bachelor of Information Technology is a Level 7 Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualification. The minimum requirements for admission are set out in the Monash University (Academic Board) Regulations.

These course outcomes are aligned with the Australian Qualifications Framework level 7 and Monash Graduate Attributes.

Upon successful completion of this course it is expected that students will be able to:

1. communicate at a professional level with clients, system users and peers

2. work effectively in a team environment

3. work independently and self-assess performance

4. apply methods, theory and research to plan, develop and implement correct, well-structured and documented information products and systems

5. act in accordance with professional codes of conduct, recognizing the social, legal and ethical consequences of their work

6. recognise the role and value of information technology in organizations and society

7. effectively use computer hardware and software technologies

8. learn and apply emerging technologies.

All applicants must satisfy the equivalence of the VCE subject prerequisites.

VET Diploma graduates: Applicants can meet the mathematics prerequisites with either a VCE mathematics subject (with appropriate score) or with an IT-related Diploma. To be considered, applicants will normally require at least a 60% average. Preference will be given to students whose prior studies are related to the course in which they are seeking admission. Programs that involve competency-based assessment without grades or marks will not meet the admission requirements. IT related diplomas may receive up to a maximum of 48 points of first year level credit.

VET Certificate IV graduates: Applicants can meet the mathematics prerequisites with either a VCE mathematics subject (with appropriate score) or with an IT-related Certificate IV. To be considered, applicants will normally require at least a 70% average. Preference will be given to students whose prior studies are related to the course in which they are seeking admission. Programs that involve competency-based assessment without grades or marks will not meet the admission requirements.

University course transfers: 

  • Applicants who already meet minimum entry requirements of the course with their previous Year 12 (or equivalent) qualification require at least two completed university units with at least a 60% average to be considered for admission. 
  • Applicants who do not meet entry requirements of the course with their previous Year 12 (or equivalent) qualification must complete at least one academic year (equivalent to eight Monash units) of university study with at least a 60% average. 
  • Applicants without the prerequisite mathematics must have undertaken at least two information technology‐related units in their current degree.

STAT: The STAT can be used to complement an applicant's overall academic background. It cannot be used as the sole pathway for admission into this course.

Bachelor of Information Technology

","honours_entry_requirements":"","overview":"

This course is about the application of computer-based technologies and systems to meet individual and organisational information needs. The course will enable you to gain the knowledge and skills needed to use IT effectively and to use, develop and manage IT-based systems. The flexibility of the course and the range of majors and minors will allow you to explore new areas, develop your strengths in IT and pursue your interests. It is a highly practical course that will prepare you for a career working with information and IT in business, government and industry.

The course covers a wide range of aspects of IT, from technical computing, which focuses on the technology itself, games and interactive media to information and business-related themes, which focus on information needs and the way in which IT can be used to support them. In addition to core studies in fundamental IT concepts, the course provides you with a choice of majors in your preferred fields of study, as well as the option to take a second major within IT or in another discipline. Knowledge and skills in IT coupled with the emphasis on generic skills problem solving, information literacy, communication and presentation skills, project management skills, and the capacity for team work will ensure that you have a firm foundation for a career in IT.

If you are an eligible student you may apply for the industry-based learning (IBL) placement program as part of the curriculum. Through the IBL placement program you will apply the skills and knowledge you have gained directly in a professional organisation.

You must complete units as specified in Parts A, B, C and D (144 points): a minimum of 96 points of information technology study over Part A and Part B, and 48 points of Elective studies (or an Innovation and Leadership major) in part C.

In choosing units you must ensure that you complete no more than 10 level one units (60 points), and at least six units (36 points) at level 3 of which at least four (24 points) are Bachelor of Information Technology listed (FIT-coded) units.

Units are 6 points unless otherwise specified.

A. Specified studies (48 points)

You must complete 48 credit points, comprising:

- core studies (36 credit points)

- applied studies (12 credit points)

Core studies

  • FIT1045 Introduction to programming
  • FIT1047 Introduction to computer systems, networks and security
  • FIT1049 IT professional practice
  • FIT2001 Systems development
  • FIT2002 IT project management
  • FIT2094 Databases

Applied studies

  • FIT3047 Industry experience studio project 1
  • FIT3048 Industry experience studio project 2

B. Major studies (48 points)

You must complete the software development major. A major requires eight units with no more than two units at level one (12 points) and at least three units (18 points) at level three. 

  • FIT1050 Web fundamentals
  • FIT1051 Programming fundamentals in java
  • FIT2081 Mobile application development
  • FIT2104 Web database interface
  • FIT2175 Usability
  • FIT3077 Software engineering: Architecture and design
  • FIT3178 iOS app development
  • FIT3184 Cloud computing

C. Elective Studies (48 points)

You must complete 48 credit points of elective units.

Electives can be chosen from across the Monash Indonesia campus, as long as you have met the prerequisites and there are no restrictions on enrolment in the units. Please note that completion of the following Innovation and Leadership units will allow you to complete a second major:

  • BEI1501 Engaging complexity
  • BEI1067 Evidence for action
  • BEI2766 Shaping futures
  • BEI2515 Catalysing change
  • BEI2500 Design thinking for global challenges
  • MGI3991 Leadership principles and practices
  • MON3500 Research, experimentation and discovery
  • MON3750 Monash innovation guarantee

If you are in a double degree course you don't complete Part C. Some units required for the other degree will be credited as electives towards this degree.

Part D. Indonesian studies (0 credit points) 

You must complete:

  • BEI1270 Indonesian studies (Religion, Indonesian language, Pancasila, and Civic Education) (0 credit points)

Note: the workload requirements (including contact hours) for each of these subjects is 2 hours per week. These units must be undertaking in parallel with your other units and cannot be completed outside Indonesia.

This is a comprehensive course, structured in four parts:

Part A. Specified studies

This will provide you with foundation skills and knowledge for your IT education and ensure a breadth of understanding of IT and its applications in organisations and society.

Part B. Major studies

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your expertise in software development. You will develop the practical and theoretical skills and knowledge needed to successfully plan, develop, implement and evaluate information products and systems.

Part C. Elective Studies

This will enable you to further develop your knowledge of the Indonesian context. You will enhance your innovative skills, cultivate your capacity for change-making, and formulate your leadership abilities.

Part D. Indonesian studies

This will enable you to gain an understating of key political, social and cultural values that define Indonesia.

Course progression map

The course progression map provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

The Bachelor of Information Technology is about the application of computer-based technologies and systems to meet individual and organisational information needs. The course will enable you to gain the knowledge and skills needed to use IT effectively and to use, develop and manage IT-based systems. It is a highly practical course that will prepare you for a career working with information and IT in business, government and industry.

The course covers a wide range of aspects of IT, from technical computing, which focuses on the technology itself, games and interactive media to information and business-related themes, which focus on information needs and the way in which IT can be used to support them. In addition to core studies in fundamental IT concepts, the course allows you to develop specialised expertise in software development. 

Knowledge and skills in IT coupled with the emphasis on generic skills problem solving, information literacy, communication and presentation skills, project management skills, and the capacity for team work will ensure that you have a firm foundation for a career in IT and/or software development.

This course comprises 48 points: Part A. Coursework (24 points) and Part B. Research (24 points)

Units are 6 points unless otherwise indicated.

Part A. Coursework studies (24 points)

You must complete:

a. the following unit:

  • FIT4005 Research methods in information technology

b. three elective units (18 points)* from level 4 or level 5 units approved by the faculty honours coordinator.

You may be permitted to do one elective unit (6 points) in selected topics (you will enrol in FIT4008 Reading unit), with permission from the thesis supervisor and honours coordinator.

* A maximum of one unit (6 points) may be selected from units offered by other faculties with the approval of the honours coordinator. 

Part B. Research studies (24 points)

You must complete:

  • FIT4441 Honours thesis part 1
  • FIT4442 Honours thesis part 2
  • FIT4443 Honours thesis part 3
  • FIT4444 Honours thesis final

","part_time":"true","structure":"

Double degree courses include the features of the component degree courses, except that electives may be reduced.

Information Technology

C2000 Bachelor of Information Technology is a comprehensive course, structured in three equal parts. In the double degree course you complete:

Part A. Specified studies

This will provide you with foundation skills and knowledge for your IT education and ensure a breadth of understanding of IT and its applications in organisations and society.

Part B. Major studies

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your expertise in one area of information technology. You will develop the practical and theoretical skills and knowledge in your chosen major needed to successfully plan, develop, implement and evaluate information products and systems.

Arts

A2000 Bachelor of Arts is a comprehensive course, structured in three equal parts. In the double degree course you complete:

Part A. Major studies

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your practical and theoretical skills and knowledge in one Faculty of Arts listed major area of study. You will learn to critically analyse, apply and communicate an advanced level of understanding of the concepts and theoretical frameworks that constitute the knowledge base of the area of study.

Part B. Specified studies

This will expose you to several arts disciplines contributing breadth to your knowledge of the arts, humanities and social sciences. You will have the flexibility of  learning about several areas of study before finalising your choice of major.  You will also build skills and abilities that employers value and seek by completing units from the Professional Futures domains. 

Course progression map

The course progression map provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

","honours_entry_requirements":"","overview":"

The globalising nature of information technology calls out for people who have both a strong technical background and an indepth understanding of human society and the factors that are shaping it.

This double degree course is designed to meet this need. As a graduate you will have the technical expertise to shape and manage current and emerging technologies together with the lifelong communication, research and critical thinking skills that are acquired through study in the arts and humanities.

Think about combining behavioural studies with business information systems to assist organisations improve their business processes. Study computer networks and security with criminology or conversely human rights or bioethics, and explore how technology confronts the boundaries between public and private. Or perhaps mix interactive media with communications and media studies or film and screen studies to add complementary skills. Or prepare yourself for an international career in IT by studying another language and culture.

Double degree courses include the features of the component degree courses, except that electives may be reduced.

Information Technology

C2000 Bachelor of Information Technology is a comprehensive course, structured in three equal parts. In the double degree course you complete:

Part A. Specified studies

This will provide you with foundation skills and knowledge for your IT education and ensure a breadth of understanding of IT and its applications in organisations and society.

Part B. Major studies

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your expertise in one area of information technology. You will develop the practical and theoretical skills and knowledge in your chosen major needed to successfully plan, develop, implement and evaluate information products and systems.

Science

S2000 Bachelor of Science is a comprehensive course, structured in three equal parts. In the double degree course you complete:

Part A. Science specified study

This will provide you with the mathematical or statistical foundation for your study of science and address the nature of science and its communication. It will also expose you to several science disciplines contributing breadth to your understanding of science and giving you the opportunity to learn about several disciplines before finalising your choice of major.

Part B. Science listed major

This will provide you with a focused program of study that will develop your expertise in one discipline area. You will learn to develop, apply and communicate an advanced level of understanding of the concepts and theoretical frameworks that constitute the knowledge base of the discipline.

Course progression map

The course progression map provides guidance on unit enrolment for each semester of study.

Applicants who have not completed VCE but have completed an IT or science-based diploma, will require an average result of at least 70%. VET Certificate IV graduates:

Applicants can meet the mathematics prerequisite of the IT degree with either a VCE mathematics subject (with appropriate score) or with an IT-related Certificate IV. For applicants who have also completed VCE, both qualifications will be considered. No credit is granted for these studies.

Applicants who do not meet minimum entry requirements of the course with their previous Year 12 (or equivalent) qualification usually must have completed at least one academic year with at least a 60% average. Previous studies must have been completed within five years of intended commencement.

Bachelor of Information Technology
Bachelor of Science

","honours_entry_requirements":"","overview":"

In an age of increasing technological advancements the synergy between science and information technology will only become stronger. IT underpins virtually all areas of science and the world needs graduates who can straddle both.

In this double degree course you will acquire creative and analytical skills to use IT to advance science. This could be anything from designing a stunning visualisation of scientific data, to building an app for fieldwork data collection to setting up the business IT processes to deliver a scientific product via the internet.

Depending on the IT major you choose, you could:

  • use your technical skills from software development to create simulations and visualisations for anything from weather forecasting to threatened species population modelling
  • apply your creative skills and design flair from interactive media or games development to create an app or game that gets kids excited about science
  • use your practical understanding of business information systems to launch a science-enabled online business
  • put your networks and security skills to work setting up the scientific instrumentation for tsunami warning or monitoring ice melts in Antarctica.

Science","associations_grouped":[],"cricos_code":"085536J","search_title":"C2003 - Bachelor of Information Technology and Bachelor of Science","other_information":"

In an age of increasing technological advancements the synergy between science and information technology will only become stronger. IT underpins virtually all areas of science and the world needs graduates who can straddle both.

In this double degree course you will acquire creative and analytical skills to use IT to advance science. This could be anything from designing a stunning visualisation of scientific data, to building an app for fieldwork data collection to setting up the business IT processes to deliver a scientific product via the internet.

Depending on the IT major you choose, you could:

  • use your technical skills from software development to create simulations and visualisations for anything from weather forecasting to threatened species population modelling
  • apply your creative skills and design flair from interactive media or games development to create an app or game that gets kids excited about science
  • use your practical understanding of business information systems to launch a science-enabled online business
  • put your networks and security skills to work setting up the scientific instrumentation for tsunami warning or monitoring ice melts in Antarctica.

You may be eligible to exit the double degree program and graduate with either a Bachelor of Information Technology (C2000) or a Bachelor of Science (S2000) after three years, depending on the units studied.

If you who wish to graduate with a Bachelor of Information Technology (C2000) prior to the completion of the double degree you must have completed at least 144 credit points of studies, including all of the requirements in Part A and B for the Bachelor of Information Technology (C2000) degree.

If you wish to graduate with a Bachelor of Science (S2000) prior to the completion of the double degree you must have completed at least 144 credit points of studies, including all of the requirements in Part A and B for the Bachelor of Science (S2000) degree.
